Polymer relaxation grows as N^1.5 to N^2 while the polymerase interval is fixed, so the
6.42e+05x margin measured at nucleosome scale is consumed somewhere between 10 and 100 kb.
THE CONCLUSION FLIPS with contour length, which is the opposite of what a single global
'relaxation is fast' claim implies.
The resolution is that 'has it relaxed' is the wrong question asked globally. A polymerase
injects TWIST locally, and local torsional equilibration is fast. What is slow is global
conformational reorganisation -- writhe redistribution, plectoneme motion. So the honest
rule is per-channel, not per-system: quasi-static stepping is valid for the LOCAL torsional
response and INVALID for long-range chain conformation, which has to be integrated or
treated as a slowly-relaxing background that the event stepper does not equilibrate.
READING
THE SEPARATION HOLDS, by 6.42e+05x. Every elastic mode in the particle has relaxed
completely before the polymerase takes its next step, so nothing is lost by refusing to
resolve the interval. Quasi-static event stepping is legitimate and the cost model's
hours-to-days figures stand on a measured foundation rather than an assumption.
The claim this licenses is narrow and worth stating exactly: it covers the ELASTIC
response of one nucleosome-scale particle. It says nothing about the slow modes of a
megabase rod, whose relaxation grows steeply with contour length and which is the
quantity that actually has to clear 30 ms at chromosome scale.
